questions.question: Explain why the factors that hinder development are described as complex and interrelated, using the resource curse and one worked chain of causes as evidence.
questions.expected_answer: No single factor explains underdevelopment; the factors form a chain in which each link pulls on the others. Access to resources, energy, history, trade imbalances, population growth, education and environmental degradation all interact: a drought cuts the harvest, so a teenager leaves school to earn, so the district's skills shrink, so investment goes elsewhere, so incomes fall, so land is overworked and the next drought bites deeper. The resource curse proves resources alone decide nothing — Angola pumps oil while most Angolans remain poor because the wealth is captured by a narrow elite, while Botswana converted its diamonds into schools, clinics and stable growth. What matters is whether resource income is turned into broad development. History adds the deepest wire: colonial borders, mine-to-harbour railways and elite-only schooling, followed in South Africa by apartheid's deliberate underdevelopment, still shape today's poverty maps. An answer that treats any one factor in isolation misses the design of the question — the marks lie in tracing the tangle.

questions.question: Describe the principles of community-based development and evaluate its potential using one rural and one urban South African case, including its limitations.
questions.expected_answer: Community-based development starts with the community rather than distant officials: the principles are participation in planning, respect for local knowledge, appropriate technology, transfer of skills so the project outlives its funders, and ownership — people maintain what is theirs. Rural case: Working for Wetlands employs local crews to plug erosion gullies and replant wetlands so catchments hold and filter water again, while workers earn wages and portable skills; the Wupperthal rooibos cooperatives in the Cederberg pool, process and market small farmers' tea jointly, keeping profits in the valley and achieving prices no lone grower could negotiate. Urban case: at Warwick Junction in Durban the city planned with its street traders, designing shelters, storage and cooking facilities around their actual trade, turning a dangerous interchange into a thriving informal economy; Enkanini's community-run solar service lit shacks before the grid arrived, and in-place upgrading of informal settlements preserves the job links and social networks that relocation destroys. The honest limits: such projects are small against national need, can be captured by local elites, and depend on patient funding — they complement state-scale delivery but cannot replace it.

questions.question: Discuss the two-way relationship between development and the environment in South Africa, and explain how sustainable development answers both directions.
questions.expected_answer: Development damages the environment: mining has left the Olifants River acidic and metal-laden, coal-fired stations make the eMalahleni airshed one of the world's dirtiest over prime maize soils, overgrazing sends topsoil into Eastern Cape dams as silt, urban sprawl covers wetlands and recharge zones, failing sewage works pollute rivers like the Hennops and Vaal, and coal dependence makes South Africa a heavy per-person carbon emitter. This damage is anti-development in the medium run — eroded soil grows less food, polluted water sickens workers, degraded land loses tourism — so destruction is a loan against development, repaid with interest, and repaid first by the poor who live nearest the damage and can least afford to move. The relationship also runs the other way: poverty degrades environments, because households without electricity strip woodland for fuel and hungry herders overstock fragile veld, deepening the poverty that caused the damage. Sustainable development answers both directions at once: meeting present needs without compromising future generations, through environmental impact assessments before major projects, binding rehabilitation duties on mines, protected areas that convert wild land into tourism income, and the shift from coal toward solar and wind energy.
